cues.en: Quick editor's note, the video you're about to watch is based on info from these three videos. One, where I slow down electricity and show that it's linked to the speed of light. A second one, where I show that electricity prefers to flow through connected wires and not disconnected wires to solve a maze. And a third one, where I try to provide an intuition for voltage current and resistance using a lot of different analogies, most notably a narrow trough of water. You don't need to have watched these videos to see this one, but if you want to learn more...
cues.zh: 快速编者按：你即将看到的视频基于这三个视频中的信息。第一个视频里，我让电变慢，并展示它与光速有关。第二个视频里，我展示电更愿意流过连通的导线，而不是断开的导线，以此解决迷宫。第三个视频里，我尝试用很多不同的类比来直观解释电压、电流和电阻，最突出的是窄水槽。你不必看过这些视频也能看懂这一期，但如果你想了解更多……

cues.en: They exist. Here, I have a very uninteresting circuit, but it's going to get a lot more interesting when recorded at ridiculously high speed. Over here, we have a battery. This is just a regular 9 volt battery, although this one's mostly dead. And although it's not plugged in yet, this is our power supply. Over here on the left, we see that the wire splits in two. The electricity from the battery could take this branch where it would meet disconnected wires.
cues.zh: 它们是存在的。这里有一个非常不起眼的电路，但以高得离谱的速度录制后，它会变得有趣得多。这边有一个电池。这只是普通的9伏电池，虽然这个基本没电了。虽然它还没接上，但这就是我们的电源。左边可以看到导线分成两路。来自电池的电可以走这个分支，那里会遇到断开的导线。

cues.en: or it could take this branch where I've soldered the wires together. Some entry-level electrical engineering tells us that of course the electric current is going to flow through the connected wires and not flow through the disconnected wires. That means we're actually going to have a loop of electrons moving. They're going to be heading away from the battery in the black wire, rounding the corner at this solder joint.
cues.zh: 或者它可以走这个分支，我已经把导线焊在一起了。入门电工学告诉我们，电流当然会流过连通的导线，而不会流过断开的导线。这意味着实际上会有一圈电子在运动。它们会在黑线中远离电池，在这个焊点处拐弯。

cues.en: and then heading towards the battery everywhere in the red wire. Over here, where the wires are disconnected, there are still electrons in the wire, but none of them should be moving because they can't go anywhere. The question I want to ask is, how do they know? Like, if I plug in this battery over here, all of a sudden, electrons are going to start, you know, chugging their way through this wire. But we know from Ohm's law that the battery voltage and the resistance of the wire should cause a very specific number of electrons to be flowing through this loop every second.
cues.zh: 然后红线各处都朝向电池前进。这边导线断开的地方，导线里仍有电子，但它们都不该移动，因为哪儿也去不了。我想问的问题是：它们怎么知道？比如，我把这边的电池接上，突然之间，电子就会开始，你知道，吭哧吭哧地穿过这根导线。但我们从欧姆定律知道，电池电压和导线电阻应该导致每秒有非常特定数量的电子流过这个回路。

cues.en: The instance I connect this battery, the other end of the circuit is a meter away. Information traveling at the speed of light takes more than three nanoseconds to traverse this setup, which means that when I plug in this battery and the battery sort of asks the universe, you know, how many electrons should I pump into the black wire every second? It takes more than six nanoseconds for it to get a reply. So what do you think is going to happen?
cues.zh: 我接上这个电池的瞬间，电路另一端在一米之外。以光速传播的信息穿过这个装置需要超过三纳秒，这意味着当我接上电池，电池有点像在问宇宙：你知道，我每秒该往黑线里泵入多少电子？它要超过六纳秒才能得到回复。那你觉得会发生什么？

cues.en: Based on comments that I've gotten on other videos, here are four possible answers. Option A, the electric field has already solved the circuit. As soon as the battery is connected, the correct amount of current will flow through the connected branch and no current will flow down the disconnected branch. Option B,
cues.zh: 根据我在其他视频收到的评论，这里有四种可能答案。选项A：电场已经解出了电路。电池一接上，正确大小的电流就会流过连通分支，而不会有电流流过断开分支。选项B，

cues.en: The electric field has already solved the circuit, but it still has to update information at the speed of light. So as soon as you connect the battery, the correct current starts to flow in the wires in a sort of bubble that expands from the connection point. Option C, the battery pumps an arbitrary amount of current into the wire, and despite one branch being disconnected, the current that's flowing splits when it gets to the fork and goes down both wires. Although this is initially wrong, it eventually stabilizes. Option D,
cues.zh: 电场已经解出了电路，但它仍必须以光速更新信息。所以电池一接上，正确电流就开始在导线中以某种从连接点扩散的气泡形式流动。选项C：电池向导线泵入任意大小的电流，尽管一个分支断开，流动的电流到达分叉处时仍会分流，沿两根导线流下去。虽然这最初是错的，但最终会稳定下来。选项D，

cues.en: Initially, nothing happens. The battery updates the electric field at the speed of light, and once information has returned from the other end of the circuit, the correct amount of current starts to flow in the connected leg all at once. In this video, we're actually going to be able to record a circuit like this fast enough to differentiate between these four options. So think about it for a minute, make your guess, and drop it in the comments while the title card plays. Are you thinking about it?
cues.zh: 最初什么也不会发生。电池以光速更新电场，一旦信息从电路另一端返回，正确大小的电流就会立刻在连通支路中开始流动。在这个视频里，我们实际上能以足够快的速度记录这样的电路，从而区分这四种选项。所以花一分钟想想，做出你的猜测，并在标题卡播放时把它发到评论里。你在想吗？

cues.en: I'm going to come back to this in more detail at the end of the video, but I wanted to give you something else to think about now. This is the branching circuit replicated using my favorite, the water channel model for electricity. Do you think that electrons in the wire will do the same thing as the water in this mock-up, despite the fact that flipping a switch is a much more dynamic system than the water model was meant to handle? You're allowed to update your guess once more before I show the real circuit in motion.
cues.zh:
我最后会在视频结尾更详细地回到这一点，但现在我想先给你们另一个可以思考的问题。
这是用我最喜欢的电流水渠模型复刻出来的分支电路。
你觉得导线里的电子会像这个演示模型里的水一样流动吗？尽管拨动开关是一个比这个水模型原本能处理的要动态得多的系统。
在我展示真实电路运行之前，你还可以再更新一次你的猜测。

cues.en: Unfortunately, observing electrons moving through wires is obscenely difficult, and I think that this is one of the reasons that electricity is so hard to learn about. I didn't properly understand the concept of line impedance, for example, until I had built the apparatus that I planned to use for this video and used it to watch waves of electricity traveling around in wires.
cues.zh: 遗憾的是，观察电子在导线中的流动极其困难，我认为这也是电学如此难学的原因之一。比如，直到我亲手做出了准备在这个视频里使用的这套装置，并用它观测到了电波在导线中来回传播，我才算真正搞懂了线路阻抗的概念。

cues.en: A regular camera, like the one on your phone, can't see electron motion. And even if it could, the changes occur on the order of the speed of light. For reference, this is a recent video from the slow-mo guys, taken at 82,000 frames per second. That sounds really fast. But in between each frame of this video, light can travel more than two miles, 3.5 kilometers. Since electricity, as in the signals and energy delivered by electric current,
cues.zh: 普通相机，比如你手机上的相机，看不到电子运动。就算能看到，这些变化也是以光速量级发生的。作为参考，这是 slow-mo guys 最近的一段视频，以每秒 82,000 帧拍摄。听起来确实很快。但在这段视频的每一帧之间，光可以传播超过两英里，也就是 3.5 公里。因为电，也就是电流所传递的信号和能量，

cues.en: travels anywhere between the speed of light and maybe half the speed of light, we clearly can't use a regular high-speed camera to observe changes in a tabletop circuit model that's only a few meters long. In fact, we're going to need to cheat even more with slower electricity and longer wires. I'm sorry for the really weird camera angle for these shots, but this literally takes up the entire room and I can only set it up on the floor unless I set it up outside. So this is what we've got.
cues.zh: 它以光速到大约半光速之间的速度传播，所以显然没法用普通高速相机去观察只有几米长的桌面电路模型里的变化。事实上，我们还得更进一步“作弊”：用更慢的电信号和更长的导线。很抱歉这些镜头机位真的很怪，但这东西几乎占满了整个房间，除非放到室外，否则我只能把它架在地板上。所以就只能这样了。

cues.en: I did try a whole bunch of methods to create extra slow transmission lines, but I ended up with this homemade twisted pair, in which electricity travels at about 60% speed of light. But since that's still too fast, I made a lot of this twisted pair, and I ended up zigzagging it onto these wooden frames, each of which holds about 23 meters of cable.
cues.zh: 我确实尝试了大量方法来制作超慢传输线，但最后还是选了这种自制的双绞线，电信号在其中的传输速度大约是光速的 60%。但由于这依然太快了，所以我做了大量的双绞线，最后把它们曲折缠绕在这些木架上，每个木架大约能缠 23 米长的线缆。

cues.en: I'll get to some of that decision-making later, like why I have this twisted pair and why my scope probes look like this. But for now, we have a larger and slower version of the circuit from the intro. At the top here, at the start of the circuit, we literally just have a 9-volt battery. And that 9-volt battery gets plugged into this circuit, which is an electronic switch, which is basically just able to plug the battery in faster than I would be able to. After that, it goes into this cable, this twisted pair.
cues.zh: 稍后我会解释其中的一些设计考量，比如为什么用这根双绞线，以及示波器探头为什么是这个样子。不过现在，我们先来看一个比开头更大、更慢的电路版本。在最上面这里，也就是电路的起点，其实就只有一个 9 伏电池。这个 9 伏电池接到了这个电路上，它是一个电子开关，作用基本上就是能比我手动接通电池的速度快得多。在那之后，它接进了这根线缆，也就是这根双绞线。

cues.en: which goes zigzagging, zigzagging, zigzagging for 23 meters into this Y where we have three cables connected and then it goes zigzagging, zigzagging over here to an open circuit where the two wires are disconnected and it goes zigzagging, zigzagging, zigzagging to here where the wires are connected which means that after this battery is plugged in we should have electric current flowing through these wires and electric current flowing through these wires where they're shorted together but we should not
cues.zh: 它一路弯弯绕绕、绕来绕去，走了23米，到这个Y形接头，这里接了三根线缆；然后它又绕来绕去，到这里的一个开路点，两根导线是断开的；接着它又绕来绕去，绕到这里，导线是连通的。这意味着电池接上后，这些导线里应该有电流流过，在被短接在一起的这些导线里也应该有电流流过；但在这里，我们不应该

cues.en: have any electricity flowing over here where the wires are disconnected. These are basically just attached but they don't really do anything. Now the round trip time at the speed of electricity is about 500 nanoseconds. When I plug in this battery or when this circuit plugs in this battery really really quickly it takes about 500 nanoseconds for that information to make it all the way to both ends of the cable and come back. That's slow enough that we should actually be able to measure it.
cues.zh: 有任何电流流过，因为这里的导线是断开的。这些线基本只是搭在一起，其实不起作用。现在，电信号往返一次的时间大约是500纳秒。当我接上这块电池——或者说这个电路接上电池——非常快，信息传到线缆两端再返回来大约要500纳秒。这慢到我们应该真的能测出来。

cues.en: The most common tool for analyzing very fast changes in electronic circuits is called an oscilloscope. I have one right here. We're going to use it in a minute. But in general, I find oscilloscopes and analysis of circuits with oscilloscopes to be very, very limiting. An oscilloscope is basically a voltmeter combined with a really accurate clock. And it will draw you a plot of...
cues.zh: 分析电子电路里极快变化的最常用工具叫示波器。我这里就有一台。我们马上会用到它。但总的来说，我觉得示波器以及用示波器分析电路非常非常有局限。示波器基本上就是电压表加一个非常精确的时钟。它会给你画出一张……

cues.en: how the voltage on a wire changes over time. For example, what if I wanted to know exactly how fast this switch is? When you plug in the battery, how quickly does the voltage on the wire go from zero to maximum? So on this plot, the x-axis is time and the y-axis is voltage. So when we plug in the battery, we can see that the voltage goes from zero to high in a very, very short span of time. This whole event takes less than 10 nanoseconds. This is a really fast switch.
cues.zh: 导线上的电压随时间如何变化的图。比如，如果我想知道这个开关到底有多快？接上电池时，导线上的电压从零升到最大值有多快？在这张图上，横轴是时间，纵轴是电压。所以接上电池时，可以看到电压在非常非常短的时间内从零变高。整个过程不到10纳秒。这真是个非常快的开关。

cues.en: In this particular case it gets a little weirder because when we zoom out we can see there's a little bit of a step right here and then there's another step right here and I mean this is just sort of bizarre like there's a dip right there before it stabilizes like what's actually going on. If you want to play this back as an animation we can imagine flipping this switch and an absurdly fast rate the voltage at this point in the circuit spikes up and then
cues.zh: 在这个例子里就更奇怪了，因为当我们缩小视图，可以看到这里有一点台阶，然后这里又有一个台阶。我是说这有点诡异，比如在稳定之前那里有个下陷。到底发生了什么？如果你想把它当成动画回放，我们可以想象以极其离谱的速度拨动这个开关，电路这一点的电压会尖峰上升，然后

cues.en: mystery stuff happens in the rest of the circuit and then the voltage over here steps down a little bit and then more mystery stuff happens in the rest of the circuit and then the voltage steps down and ends up stabilizing. This is why I find oscilloscope traces so limiting. You can see what's happening at one location, but you can't really see everything. The trick that we can use is to probe more points on the circuit at once.
cues.zh: 电路其余部分发生一些神秘现象，然后这里的电压下降一点，接着电路其余部分又发生更多神秘现象，然后电压再下降，最后稳定下来。这就是为什么我觉得示波器波形这么有局限。你能看到一个位置发生的事情，但没法真正看到全貌。我们可以用的技巧是同时探测电路上更多的点。

cues.en: If I take an extra set of scope probes and I attach them in the middle, now we see something very interesting. The voltage at this point in the circuit doesn't rise until 116 nanoseconds later. If I measure the voltage at this point, at the end where the wires are connected together, we basically see, oh man, it's very noisy. Hot, hot. Let's melt my fingers together, that'll help. If I measure the voltage at the end of the circuit that shorted out, where the wires are just soldered together,
cues.zh: 如果我再拿一组示波器探头接到中间，现在就会看到很有意思的事。电路这个点的电压要等到 116 纳秒之后才上升。如果我测量这个点——也就是导线接在一起的那一端——基本会看到，哎呀，噪声非常大。好烫，好烫。干脆把我的手指熔在一起吧，也许能管用。如果我测量短路那部分电路的末端——也就是导线直接焊在一起的地方，

cues.en: we can see on the scope that the voltage basically stays flat the whole time. But now requiring me to be completely under the table, if we measure the voltage over here, if we wait about 240 nanoseconds, then we see the voltage at this point all the way at the end of the wire start to go up. So let's run that same visualization again. When we flip this switch, we see the voltage at the switch go up.
cues.zh: 我们能在示波器上看到，电压基本一直保持不变。但现在我得整个人钻到桌子底下，如果我们测量这边的电压，等大约 240 纳秒，就会看到导线最末端这个点的电压开始上升。那我们再把同一个可视化跑一遍。当我们合上开关，会看到开关处的电压上升。

cues.en: and then something happens probably in the first panel, and then we see the voltage go up in the middle, and then something happens probably in both panels, and then we see something happen in the panel with the disconnected wires, which was the panel where we didn't expect to see anything happening. Then we just started to see voltages changing all over the circuit. It's not super clear what's going on.
cues.zh: 然后第一个面板里可能发生了点什么，接着我们看到中间的电压上升，然后两个面板里可能都发生了点什么，再然后我们看到断开的导线所在的那个面板也发生了点事情——而那个面板原本我们没指望会看到任何变化。然后我们开始看到整个电路各处的电压都在变化。到底发生了什么，还不太清楚。

cues.en: This is why I get frustrated with oscilloscopes as a learning tool sometimes, because you can't see the propagation. So with a couple extremely tedious hours of stripping wires with an exacto knife, I added taps every four feet so that I could attach probes all over the place and play them back at the same time. This ends us with something that looks like this. If I show it in a more graphy view here, maybe some of these features get clearer. I really love this footage and it shows that no, the battery has no idea
cues.zh: 这就是为什么作为学习工具，示波器有时让我很沮丧，因为你看不到传播过程。所以，我用美工刀剥线，花了极其枯燥的几个小时，每隔四英尺加一个抽头，这样我就能到处接探头，并同时把它们回放出来。最后得到的东西看起来像这样。如果我在这里用更图形化的视图展示，也许其中一些特征会更清楚。我真的很喜欢这段画面，它说明：不，电池根本不知道

cues.en: how much current should flow when you plug it in. The battery is connected, a whole bunch of current flows down the wire. When it hits the Y, the current gets split, but also something looks like it reflects back towards the battery. That's kind of weird. And now we have a pulse, actually two identical pulses traveling down both far wires. Remember, this wire has the ends disconnected and this wire has the ends soldered together. When the two identical pulses reach the end of their respective wires,
cues.zh: 插上之后应该流多少电流。电池一接通，一大堆电流就沿着导线流下去。当它碰到 Y 形接头时，电流会分流，但同时也似乎有什么东西反射回电池那边。这有点奇怪。现在我们有一个脉冲，实际上是两个完全相同的脉冲，沿着两条远端导线传播。记住，这条导线末端是断开的，而这条导线末端是焊在一起的。当这两个完全相同的脉冲到达各自导线的末端时，

cues.en: The one that meets a disconnected circuit slams into a wall. All of that current sloshes back and piles up. The other pulse gets shorted out, drops to zero, and also sends that information back towards the battery.
cues.zh: 遇到断开电路的那个脉冲会像撞墙一样撞上去。所有那些电流会涌回来并堆积起来。另一个脉冲则被短路，降到零，同时也把这个信息送回电池那边。

cues.en: If I speed up here, we see over a few reflections, the battery realizes it tried to send way too much power the first time, and slowly the whole circuit settles down. Current, the actual flow of electrons, ends up following this slope, as the high voltage at the battery drops to nothing at the short, and in the disconnected wire, where nothing should be happening, there isn't a slope.
cues.zh: 如果我在这里加速，经过几次反射后，会看到电池意识到它第一次试图送出太多功率，然后整个电路慢慢稳定下来。电流，也就是电子的实际流动，最终沿着这个斜率变化：电池处的高电压在短路处降到零；而在断开的那根导线里，本不该发生什么，也就没有斜率。

cues.en: no voltage to make electrons move. Until the waves actually get to the ends of the wire, they look identical. Because these waves of current don't know what is at the end of their respective branches of the circuit. Once they realize what's at the end of their circuit, they transmit that information back to the battery. This branch says, whoa, I need a bit less current this way. It looks like a wall. And this one says, hey, I need more current. Make this hill a little bit steeper.
cues.zh: 没有电压推动电子移动。直到这些波真正到达导线末端之前，它们看起来完全相同。因为这些电流波不知道自己所在电路各分支的末端是什么。一旦它们弄清所在电路的末端是什么，就会把这一信息传回电池。这个分支说：哇，这边我需要少一点电流，它看起来像一堵墙。而另一个说：嘿，我需要更多电流，把这个坡弄得再陡一点。

cues.en: When both these signals meet each other and eventually get back to the battery, there's a negotiation, and it requires a lot of back and forth communication. In this case, the whole circuit took about 4,000 nanoseconds to stabilize. That's like eight round trips. I also want to point out that these wires can't talk to each other through this gap.
cues.zh: 当这两个信号相遇并最终回到电池时，会发生一次协商，需要大量来回通信。在这种情况下，整个电路花了大约4000纳秒才稳定下来。这大概相当于八个往返。我还想指出，这些导线无法通过这个间隙相互通信。

cues.en: I just wanted to make it easy to compare the waves by putting them side by side. So for those of you keeping score at home, the answer is C. It takes much longer than one round trip for electricity, for the current to stabilize, and for the circuit to obey Ohm's law in DC. But that leaves us with a few more questions. Like, what are these waves that are traveling through this circuit? And how does the battery and...
cues.zh: 我只是想把它们并排放好，方便比较这些波。所以，对于在家记分的朋友们，答案是 C。要让电信号、让电流稳定下来，并让电路在直流下遵守欧姆定律，所需时间远不止一个往返。但这还留下几个问题。比如，这些在电路中传播的波到底是什么？以及电池和……

cues.en: switch assembly here decide how much current should initially flow in the wire if it's just guessing and it doesn't know how much current should flow to either end. To answer those questions I have a similar but simpler circuit set up here. Instead of a big branching circuit with lots and lots of wire this is just a straight shot. So I have the same very fast electronic switch that plugs the battery into the wire and then I have
cues.zh: 这里的开关组件如何决定最初应该有多少电流流入导线，如果它只是在猜测，并不知道应该有多少电流流向两端。为了回答这些问题，我在这里搭了一个类似但更简单的电路。这里不是有很多很多导线的大型分支电路，而是一条直线路径。所以我有同样非常快的电子开关，把电池接入导线，然后我有

cues.en: 23 meters of my custom twisted pair and at the end two wires that are dangling free so that I can attach whatever resistor I want as a load on the end of this circuit. That basically means that we have a power supply and we have a load that are separated by hundreds of nanoseconds of delay time.
cues.zh: 23米长的自制双绞线，末端有两根悬空的导线，这样我就可以把任意电阻作为负载接到这个电路的末端。这基本上意味着，我们有一个电源和一个负载，它们之间隔着数百纳秒的延迟时间。

cues.en: It's really easy to go in here and say, I know the resistance of the wire. I know the resistance of the load. I know the resistance that's built into the power supply. And you can calculate how much current, literally how many electrons per second, are going to be chugging their way through this wire.
cues.zh: 很容易在这里直接说：我知道导线的电阻。我知道负载的电阻。我知道电源内置的电阻。然后你可以计算出会有多少电流，字面意义上每秒有多少电子，吭哧吭哧地穿过这根导线。

cues.en: As we just saw, the correct number of electrons don't flow the first time you hit the switch. They sort of have to bounce around and figure it out. For the first test, I'm just going to short out the end. I've soldered these two wires together, so this big long chain is terminated in a zero ohm resistor. I spent what ended up being quite a while writing a script that brings in these voltage traces and produces an exaggerated view of how the electrons actually move in the wire.
cues.zh: 正如我们刚才看到的，第一次合上开关时，流动的电子数量并不正确。它们得来回弹一弹，自己摸索出来。第一次测试，我直接把末端短路。我把这两根线焊在一起，所以这条长链的终端是一个零欧姆电阻。我花了相当长的时间写脚本，导入这些电压波形，并把电子在导线中实际如何移动做成夸张的可视化。

cues.en: So I want to be very clear, this top plot is real data that I actually collected. This is 20 individual oscilloscope traces that are all being played back at the same time. And this is a heavily exaggerated animation of the electron's motion based on that data. And then this final plot is a realistic, albeit extremely noisy, graph of electron drift velocity along the wire's length that we'll talk about in a minute, but it's also based on the raw data. For now, let's cover most of this up.
cues.zh: 我想说清楚，顶部这张图是我实际采集的真实数据。这是 20 条独立的示波器波形，正在同时回放。而这是基于这些数据、对电子运动做了高度夸张的动画。最后这张图是沿导线长度的电子漂移速度图，虽然噪声极大，但它是真实的，也基于原始数据，我们稍后会讲。现在先把大部分遮起来。

cues.en: The fundamental point here is the speed of electricity and the speed of the electrons, and those are not the same thing. If we look at this way of traveling down the wire, we see that it travels this 23 meters in about 120 nanoseconds, which means it's traveling at almost 200,000 kilometers per second, which is like two-thirds the speed of light. That is absurdly fast. However, if we look at these electrons that have started moving, they go a whole lot slower.
cues.zh: 核心点是电的速度和电子的速度，它们不是一回事。看这种沿导线传播的方式，它用大约 120 纳秒走完这 23 米，意味着速度接近每秒 20 万公里，约为光速的三分之二。这快得离谱。但看这些已经开始移动的电子，它们慢得多。

cues.en: In the graphic, the individual electrons are moving about 10 times slower than the wave. And that right there is the exaggeration because in reality, the electrons in this wire are traveling about 10 trillion times slower than the wave. But that doesn't make for a very understandable graphic. But if they were drawn out accurately, you'd never be able to see that they were scrunched in some places and more spread out in other places because the spacing just doesn't change very much. That said, it is...
cues.zh: 图中单个电子比波慢约 10 倍。这正是夸张之处，因为现实中这根导线里的电子比波慢约 10 万亿倍。但那样图就不容易看懂了。不过如果按真实比例画，你永远看不出它们在有些地方挤在一起、另一些地方更分散，因为间距变化实在太小。话虽如此，正是……

cues.en: the scrunching and spreading out of electrons in different parts of wires that causes electrons to do what they do and flow through wires. If we look at the wires, these are the two wires of the twisted pair, although the twist really doesn't matter. When we flip the switch and this wave travels down the wire, we see that the electrons are pulled from one wire and shoved into the other. But at the end, the electrons haven't started moving yet.
cues.zh: 导线不同部分中电子的挤压和散开，才使电子表现出这些行为并流过导线。看这些导线，这是双绞线的两根线，虽然绞合其实并不重要。当我们合上开关，这个波沿导线传播时，会看到电子被从一根线拉出、推入另一根线。但在远端，电子还没开始移动。

cues.en: Any given point on this trace at the top is the voltage or potential difference between the wires of the twisted pair below. When this voltage goes up here, but is still zero over here, we're saying that in this region, there are more electrons in the wire than this wire. But at the far end, there are just as many electrons in both wires. Of course, this is about to change. As this wave reaches the end of the wire, all these electrons start moving. So in answer to our first question, what are these waves? These waves are waves of motion.
cues.zh: 顶部波形上任意一点，都是下方双绞线两根导线之间的电压或电势差。当这里的电压升高，而那边仍为零，就表示在这个区域，这根导线里的电子比那根多。但在远端，两根导线里的电子一样多。当然，这马上会改变。当波到达导线末端，所有这些电子开始移动。所以回答第一个问题：这些波是什么？这些波是运动的波。

cues.en: and waves of electron bunching and scrunching. At one instant, if there are electrons moving to the right in this part of the wire and not moving in this other part of the wire, the only way that can be happening is if the electrons in between those two regions in this part of the wire are actually getting closer together. And if we play this footage forwards, that's exactly what we see. It's a common argument in my comment section that these waves of electricity are just the electric field and that the electrons don't really move.
cues.zh: 以及电子聚束和挤压的波。某一瞬间，如果导线这一部分有电子向右运动，而另一部分没有电子运动，那么唯一可能的情况是：这两片区域之间的电子实际上正在彼此靠近。把这段画面向前播放，看到的正是这样。我的评论区常有一种说法：这些电波只是电场，电子并没有真正移动。

cues.en: But if that were the case, this zigzag layout wouldn't work. The electric field would cover the whole panel faster than I'd be able to measure it. These phenomena only make sense if electrons are actually scooching down the wire and bunching up, even if ever so slightly. That's why electricity follows wires and cables. It can only go where the electrons can scooch forwards. I originally had this circuit set up where the wires at the end were shorted together, so it was basically like a zero ohm resistor.
cues.zh: 但如果是那样，这个锯齿形布局就不会起作用。电场会以我根本来不及测量的速度覆盖整块板。只有电子确实沿着导线挪动并聚拢起来——哪怕幅度极小——这些现象才说得通。这就是为什么电会沿着导线和电缆走。它只能去电子能向前挪动的地方。我最初搭这个电路时，把末端的导线短接在一起，所以基本上相当于一个零欧姆电阻。

cues.en: But now, I've cut them apart. So there's an infinity ohm resistor right here where the two wires are just, you know, hanging free. So what do you think is going to happen in this case? There's no way for electrons to flow down the black wire all the way down to the end, somehow magically jump this gap, and flow back along the red wire. But we know that when we flip this switch...
cues.zh: 但现在，我把它们切开了。所以这里就相当于一个无穷大欧姆电阻，两根导线只是悬空在那里。那你觉得这种情况下会发生什么？电子不可能沿着黑线一路流到末端，然后神奇地跳过这个间隙，再沿红线流回去。但我们知道，当我们合上这个开关……

cues.en: We're going to have current. Electrons are going to start moving in this part of the wire the moment we flip this switch. So what's that going to look like when it gets to the end? It's going to look like this. After we flip the switch, we get the exact same step. The same wave of electricity at about two and a quarter volts of potential and about 15 milliamps of current are flowing in that part of the wire. But when that wave gets to the end, it can't go anywhere.
cues.zh: 我们会得到电流。我们一合上开关，导线这一部分的电子就会开始移动。那当它到达末端时会是什么样？会是这样。合上开关后，我们得到完全相同的阶跃。同样的电波，大约 2.25 伏电势、15 毫安电流，在导线那部分流动。但当这个波到达末端时，它无处可去。

cues.en: Basically, these electrons slam into the end of the wire and pile up. Now, we have a big, steep slope of voltage in the other direction. If the first slope accelerated electrons towards the load, this reverse slope decelerates the electrons, and awesomely, the magnitudes match. So, all the electrons start moving, then the reflected wave perfectly cancels them out, and they all stop moving. Of course, it does bounce back and forth a bit more, but after all that,
cues.zh: 基本上，这些电子撞到导线末端并堆积起来。现在，我们得到了一个方向相反、又大又陡的电压斜坡。如果第一个斜坡把电子加速推向负载，那么这个反向斜坡就会让电子减速，而且很妙的是，幅度正好匹配。于是，所有电子开始移动，然后反射波完美地将它们抵消，它们全都停了下来。当然，它还会再来回反弹几次，但经过这一切之后，

cues.en: we end up with two wires full of unmoving electrons. The fact that at the end of this animation, this extremely data-driven animation, all of the electrons stop moving, like, makes me so happy. The fact that the wave going one way is perfectly canceled by the wave going the other way when it hits the end of this is so cool. And that can be measured accurately enough to make an animation like this with an oscilloscope that's only a few hundred bucks. Just...
cues.zh: 最后我们得到两根充满静止电子的导线。这个动画——这个完全由数据驱动的动画——到最后所有电子都停下来，这让我特别开心。一个方向传播的波在到达末端时，被另一个方向的波完美抵消，这实在太酷了。而且用一台只要几百美元的示波器，就能测得足够精确，做出这样的动画。只是……

cues.en: I was so excited when I saw this animation for the first time. But both wires are at different potentials. There's a voltage difference between them. If you want to get technical, we're now seeing the wires capacitance measured in charge per volt. Physically, how many charged electrons we need to add to a wire to change its voltage. This also, in a roundabout way, answers our second question.
cues.zh: 我第一次看到这个动画时特别兴奋。但两根导线处于不同电势，它们之间存在电压差。如果你想说得专业一点，我们现在看到的是导线的电容，以每伏特电荷量来衡量。从物理上说，就是需要往导线里加入多少个带电电子，才能改变它的电压。这还间接回答了我们的第二个问题。

cues.en: In both cases, the exact same wave left from the battery, because the circuit at this end didn't yet know what was at this end. And the magnitude of this wave was largely controlled by the capacitance of the wire. How many electrons can be crammed into this wire when you apply a certain voltage? Or to be linguistic about it, the wire's capacity to hold extra electrons.
cues.zh: 在这两种情况下，从电池出发的都是完全相同的波，因为这一端的电路还不知道那一端是什么。而这个波的幅度很大程度上由导线的电容决定。施加一定电压时，能往这根导线里塞进多少个电子？或者用更语言学的方式说，就是导线容纳额外电子的能力。

cues.en: This value is very high for instances like this where you have nearby wires wrapped in insulation and extremely low for wires that are far apart with nothing in between. So now let's go back to the Y-shaped circuit and hopefully you'll see all these effects present in a much more complicated model. So now we understand this first bit. When we send a pulse of voltage down the wire, at the ends of the branches the electrons aren't moving yet. But everywhere this wave has been...
cues.zh: 像这种情况，导线彼此靠近且包有绝缘层，这个值会非常高；而导线相距很远、中间什么都没有时，这个值又极低。现在让我们回到 Y 形电路，希望你能在一个复杂得多的模型里看到所有这些效应。现在我们理解了开头这一小段。当我们沿导线发送一个电压脉冲时，在各分支的末端，电子还没有开始移动。但在这个波已经到达的所有地方……

cues.en: electrons have started moving. And at the edge of the wave, the electrons are either clumping up or spreading out. Now when this pulse hits the fork, three things happen. Part of the wave reflects back, part of the wave continues into the connected branch, and part of the wave continues into the disconnected branch.
cues.zh: 电子已经开始移动。而在波的前沿，电子要么聚集起来，要么散开。现在，当这个脉冲到达分叉点时，会发生三件事。一部分波反射回去，一部分波继续进入连接着的分支，还有一部分波继续进入未连接的分支。

cues.en: These waves continue until they hit their respective loads, a dead short or zero ohm resistor, and an open circuit or infinity ohm resistor. Just like in the single cable test, we see the electrons that hit the open circuit pile up and reflect back, stopping all motion. And in the other branch, the wave reflects back low, actually accelerating the electrons in the wire.
cues.zh: 这些波会继续传播，直到碰到各自的负载：一个是完全短路，也就是零欧电阻；另一个是开路，也就是无穷欧电阻。就像在单根电缆测试中一样，我们看到撞上开路的电子会堆积起来并反射回去，停止所有运动。而在另一个分支中，波以低电平反射回来，实际上还加速了导线中的电子。

cues.en: further. This branching circuit is a dramatically more complicated system than the single cable terminated in a resistor, but hopefully you can see the same patterns in both. We can continue tracing individual reflections and waves and interactions between electrons in all of these wires and carefully predicting what will happen next, or we can just fast forward to the end and see that all of this hardly matters because after a few hundred nanoseconds everything settles out and we get exactly what we expect.
cues.zh: 进一步。这个分支电路比单根终端接电阻的电缆复杂得多，但希望你能在两者中看到相同的模式。我们可以继续追踪所有这些导线中的各个反射、波以及电子之间的相互作用，并仔细预测接下来会发生什么；或者我们可以直接快进到结尾，看到这一切几乎都不重要，因为几百纳秒后一切都会稳定下来，我们得到的结果完全符合预期。

cues.en: a descending gradient from power supply to load where the DC version of Ohm's law is satisfied for all locations. This is the same net result I measured in the electricity maze video but at that scale I wasn't able to record it fast enough to show you how it got that way. Hopefully now it makes a little more sense and you can imagine these waves sort of percolating through every possible way to solve that maze at once before the circuit settled into that result.
cues.zh: 从电源到负载的下降梯度，在所有这些位置上，直流版本的欧姆定律都成立。这与我在“电力迷宫”视频中测得的最终结果相同，但在那个尺度上，我没法足够快地记录下来，向你展示它是怎么变成这样的。希望现在这能更容易理解一点，你可以想象这些波同时渗透过解决那个迷宫的每一种可能路径，然后电路才稳定到那个结果。

cues.en: At the start I mentioned the water channel model was going to make a comeback and I want to show you what parts of the water channel model are applicable and where you have to be careful. And then somewhere we got one down there. Is it only three leaks? It's pretty great. I recreated the circuit as best I could with acrylic sheet water channels and used large basins of water as a supply and a load. So effectively we have two capacitors connected to ground, a switch, and an extra bit of wire. So check out these shots side by side.
cues.zh: 开头我提到水渠模型会回归，我想展示水渠模型哪些部分适用，哪些地方需要小心。然后我们在下面某处弄到了一个。只有三个漏点吗？挺棒的。我用亚克力板水渠尽可能复现了这个电路，并用大盆水作为电源和负载。所以实际上我们有两个接地电容、一个开关和一小段额外的导线。来看看这些并排镜头。

cues.en: In both cases, the wave leaves from the supply, travels down the first leg, splits at the branch, sloshes up at the dead end, and sloshes down at the open end. The fact that this water channel model is able to so accurately depict the dynamics of electricity, a completely different system, and one that operates on time scales that are orders of magnitude faster than water, it's just really amazing to me. But it's not perfect.
cues.zh: 两种情况下，波都从电源出发，沿第一段传播，在分支处分开，在封闭端涌起，在开口端落下。这个水渠模型能如此准确地描绘电的动态——一个完全不同的系统，而且其时间尺度比水快几个数量级——这对我来说真的非常神奇。但它并不完美。

cues.en: Weirdly, in the water version, the back reflections aren't as pronounced. When the signals hit the loads at the end, we absolutely see one wave pile up and the other drop low. But in general, the dynamics of water are a little more direct, and the signals returning to the power supply aren't as obvious. One reason for this may be that the parameters of the circuits don't match. If I repeat the electricity experiment with higher resistance wire, not impedance, but resistance, we get a slightly closer analog, where the reflections of
cues.zh: 奇怪的是，在水版本中，反向反射没那么明显。当信号到达末端的负载时，我们确实看到一列波堆积，另一列波变低。但总的来说，水的动态更直接一些，返回电源的信号也不那么明显。原因之一可能是电路参数不匹配。如果我用电阻更高的导线重复电实验——不是阻抗，而是电阻——我们会得到稍微更接近的类比，其中电的反射

cues.en: electricity are significantly diminished. But while water in a narrow channel and electrons in a wire do show a lot of similarities, like seriously I can keep listing them for 40 minutes, inertia is something that's really finicky. If you look at this model from above you can see that it's not symmetrical and neither is it straight. The way that water maintains inertia around corners is extremely different from electrons which pick up an effective inertia while drifting by creating a magnetic field around the wire.
cues.zh: 会显著减弱。不过，虽然窄渠中的水和导线中的电子确实有很多相似之处——说真的，我可以连续列上40分钟——但惯性这件事真的很微妙。如果你从上方看这个模型，会发现它既不对称，也不直。水在拐角处保持惯性的方式，与电子截然不同；电子在漂移时会通过在导线周围产生磁场而获得一种有效惯性。

cues.en: This divot, for example, would never appear in electron flow in a wire. And at the end, I wasn't able to create a perfect low voltage supply to pull the signal down. But this is something that's really easy in wires. I always imagine circuits, even dynamic ones with waves, like water flowing through these channels. But sometimes the mental image with the idealized water flowing down an idealized water trough is...
cues.zh: 比如这个凹坑，在导线中的电子流里绝不会出现。到最后，我也没能做出一个完美的低压电源来把信号拉低。但这在导线中非常容易。我总把电路——即使是带波动的动态电路——想象成水流过这些渠道。但有时候，理想化的水沿理想化水槽流下的这个心理图像是……

cues.en: a better analog to electricity than building one in real life and filming it in real life. However, even this real one with all of its imperfections is an excellent qualitative model that I think provides a lot of intuition for an otherwise very difficult topic.
cues.zh: 比在现实中造一个并拍摄它更好的电学类比。不过，即便是这个有种种缺陷的真实模型，也是一个极好的定性模型，我认为它能为一个原本非常困难的主题提供大量直觉。

cues.en: Of course, what actually happens in my head is that when this doesn't match I start thinking of a more complicated electronic circuit that would match this better. Like this milk jug at the end is basically a capacitor and the fact that I've cut it off makes it a voltage regulator and it's a lot better than basically what I had before was like a voltage sensitive resistor where I just ended it. Anyway, I hope that you learned something about electricity watching this video. I certainly learned a lot about electricity.
cues.zh: 当然，我脑子里实际发生的是：当这个模型对不上时，我就开始想一个更复杂的电子电路，让它更贴合。比如最后这个牛奶壶基本上就是个电容，而我把它剪开这一点让它成了稳压器，这比我之前的基本做法好多了——之前我只是把它末端接上，像是个压敏电阻。总之，希望你看这个视频学到了一些电学知识。我肯定学到了很多电学知识。

cues.en: making this video and had a lot of fun trying to figure out how to film electricity at a ridiculous speed and making the equivalent water model to think about.
